scope.design: purposive exploratory survey; not field prevalence estimate
scope.raw_policy: All source publications, tool renderings, OCR and mechanical extracts remain local-only. Original summaries/code/metadata are authored artifacts.
scope.access_rule: A complete acquired file does not mean complete reading. Inspected scope is explicitly declared for every work.
scope.followup: L28 added after the initial census because L26 explicitly names it as a direct integration predecessor.
scope.inherited_sources: L22/L23/L27 reuse review-agent witnesses; L24/L26 reuse coordinator witnesses. Independent selected reading is declared; no duplicate acquisition.

sources.title: The Urban Revolution
sources.inspected_scope: Title and opening p3; selected printed pp11–12 and16–17, PDF14–15 and19–20. Article occupies pp3–17; intervening plates cause the PDF offset.
sources.mechanism_summary: Specialists depend on surplus and exchange; metalworking cities can depend on distant raw materials and complementary producers.
sources.author_recommendation: No distinct future-research prescription extracted from the selected passages.
sources.interpretive_limit: The historical typology assumes centralized surplus and other institutions. Its dated claims about Harappan palaces/granaries are not adopted as excavation evidence.

sources.title: Social complexity and sustainability
sources.inspected_scope: Title/abstract and introductory pp91–92; selected conclusions and strategic responses pp99–101, PDF9–11. No complete reanalysis of the historical cases.
sources.mechanism_summary: Problem solving can accumulate costs; subsidies, deferred expenditure and information arrangements change how those costs are borne.
sources.author_recommendation: Become aware of accumulated costs, examine subsidies and deferred costs, connect costs with benefits through effective information, and reconsider expensive problem-solving arrangements.
sources.interpretive_limit: The selected argument supplies conditional cost mechanisms, not an inevitable collapse trajectory or a fitted ancient cost curve.

sources.title: Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems
sources.citation: Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 4:1–23; IIASA reprint RP-73-003
sources.work_type: original ecological theory and case synthesis
sources.inspected_scope: Introduction printed pp1–2/PDF5–6 and synthesis pp17–20/PDF21–24; complete report acquired but remaining pages not claimed read.
sources.mechanism_summary: Persistence of relationships can coexist with variation; stability around one equilibrium and survival through disturbance are separate properties.
sources.author_recommendation: Management should preserve options, heterogeneity and capacity to accommodate change, with attention to regional dispersal and uncertain system structure.
sources.interpretive_limit: The ecological cases do not establish a universal urban cycle or an archaeological survival probability.

sources.title: Understanding the Complexity of Economic, Ecological, and Social Systems
sources.inspected_scope: Title/abstract; selected printed p394 and pp398–400, PDF5 and9–11. Primary article reproduced on an NGO host; host is not the publisher.
sources.mechanism_summary: Potential, connectedness and adaptive capacity interact across scales; accumulated skills, trust and networks affect reorganization.
sources.author_recommendation: Use cross-scale relationships and opportunities for experiment and reorganization in understanding adaptive change.
sources.interpretive_limit: The adaptive cycle is a heuristic; the selected material does not justify assigning every society a fixed four-stage chronology.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Resilience, Adaptability and Transformability in Social–ecological Systems
sources.inspected_scope: Publisher HTML introduction and definitions of resilience, adaptability and transformability; retained text lines72–97. Later explanatory cases are outside the declared reading.
sources.mechanism_summary: Actors can adjust within a regime or form a different system when the existing arrangement becomes untenable.
sources.author_recommendation: Define the system, its state variables and desired outcome before assessing resilience and transformation.
sources.interpretive_limit: A change that preserves residents or livelihoods can end a particular institutional or urban configuration.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Resilience Thinking: Integrating Resilience, Adaptability and Transformability
sources.inspected_scope: Glossary/table on PDF3 and selected text on PDF4–7: specified/general resilience, transformation across scales and conclusion.
sources.mechanism_summary: Small-scale transformation can support larger-scale persistence; experiments, learning and alternatives can alter what continues.
sources.author_recommendation: Attend to general resilience and to learning and transformation across scales, beyond responses to one specified shock.
sources.interpretive_limit: The retained PDF has article pagination rather than ordinary journal page numbers; its case summaries were not independently reanalyzed.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: A Framework to Analyze the Robustness of Social-ecological Systems from an Institutional Perspective
sources.inspected_scope: Selected publisher introduction/framework and interactions at operational/collective-choice levels; retained text lines215–256 for the latter.
supporting_loci: Interactions at operational and collective-choice levels
sources.mechanism_summary: Resources, users, infrastructure and infrastructure providers form linked relationships; provider-user feedback affects contributions and maintenance.
sources.author_recommendation: Examine links and incentives connecting users with public infrastructure providers and specify boundary and time scale.
sources.interpretive_limit: A focal resource can decline while users substitute another resource; robustness is relative to the chosen outcome and boundary.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: A General Framework for Analyzing Sustainability of Social-Ecological Systems
sources.inspected_scope: Article title/abstract p419 and selected leading text on pp420–422; PDF2–5 contains the article, with the end of a preceding article above its title on PDF2.
sources.mechanism_summary: Resource systems, units, users and governance interact; group size has different effects depending on transaction costs and management work.
sources.author_recommendation: Build comparable quantitative and qualitative databases with nested variables, heterogeneous costs/benefits and explicit spatial and temporal scales.
sources.interpretive_limit: The framework supports diagnosis and comparison; the selected cross-case summaries do not identify an ancient governance form.

sources.title: The persistence of ancient settlements and urban sustainability
sources.citation: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118:e2018155118
sources.work_type: archaeological conceptual synthesis and illustrative comparisons
sources.inspected_scope: JATS body paragraphs7–30 and31–34: outcome types, duration/data problems and research agenda. Europe PMC XML replaces a failed PMC challenge; no supporting dataset reanalysis.
sources.mechanism_summary: Occupation, population scale, institutions and culture can persist differently; geography, demography and collective action are candidate explanations.
sources.author_recommendation: Standardize archaeological data, assemble interdisciplinary comparisons and develop theory connecting settlement duration with institutional, demographic and geographic features.
sources.interpretive_limit: Illustrative duration figures are not a complete random settlement sample. Selected main text supplies no quantified initial stocks, import limits or repair schedules.
sources.rights_observation: Observed CC BY-NC-ND4.0 notice in primary JATS; raw/derivatives kept local-only

sources.title: Housing inequality and settlement persistence are associated across the archaeological record
sources.citation: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122:e2400696122
sources.inspected_scope: Primary main-text web rendering and JATS Methods paragraphs22–24, Results paragraph6, Discussion selected paragraphs16–18 and Outlook paragraphs20–21. No dataset/model rerun.
sources.mechanism_summary: Housing area disparity, settlement scale and occupation duration are compared; the associations do not establish a universal inequality threshold.
sources.author_recommendation: Use complete settlement systems to distinguish network-wide gains from extraction benefiting some settlements at others expense.
sources.interpretive_limit: Duration can miss contractions or short gaps. The study does not estimate the service demand, stock/output ceiling and import ceiling needed for our proposed bound.
sources.rights_observation: Observed CC BY4.0 notice in primary JATS; raw/derivatives kept local-only

sources.title: Integrating adaptation pathways and Ostrom’s framework for sustainable governance of social-ecological systems in a changing world
sources.work_type: original integrated formal framework and modeled application
sources.inspected_scope: Primary introduction and Table1; JATS selected paragraphs14,31–38,85–87,91–95,99–101. Coupled pathways and concluding limitations inspected; full numerical experiment not reproduced.
sources.mechanism_summary: Nested collective/constitutional actions alter viable pathways in coupled systems, with providers, institutions, infrastructure, knowledge and external assistance represented.
sources.author_recommendation: Include incremental costs of moving between constitutional/collective arrangements; distinguish service preferences, changing environment and institutions in practical applications.
sources.interpretive_limit: This is a close direct predecessor. The authors report insufficient transition-cost data; a feasible modeled pathway does not authenticate an ancient sequence.
sources.rights_observation: Observed primary JATS Creative Commons Attribution notice; raw/derivatives kept local-only

sources.title: Demography and Cultural Evolution: How Adaptive Cultural Processes Can Produce Maladaptive Losses—The Tasmanian Case
sources.work_type: original cultural-learning model and historical application
sources.inspected_scope: Abstract printed p197/PDF2 and selected model pp200–202/PDF5–7; model assumptions and effective interacting population read. Historical archaeological claims not independently audited.
sources.mechanism_summary: Under the declared biased/noisy social-learning law, access to a larger interacting skill pool can offset transmission loss.
sources.author_recommendation: The selected abstract speculates about applying the model to variability in adaptive cultural evolution; no separately inspected research-design prescription extracted.
sources.interpretive_limit: Model-specific thresholds do not identify a universal minimum population. The historical Tasmanian interpretation remains an author application, not a new result here.

sources.title: Partial connectivity increases cultural accumulation within groups
sources.citation: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(11):2982–2987
sources.inspected_scope: Abstract/design printed pp2982–2983, results pp2984–2985 and discussion/Methods opening p2986, PDF1–5. Remaining detailed methods not claimed read.
sources.mechanism_summary: In a path-dependent computer task, partial connectivity preserved diverse solution branches that could later recombine; complete connection fostered early convergence.
sources.author_recommendation: Investigate learning structure, fitness landscapes and contacts among partially separated groups when explaining cultural accumulation.
sources.interpretive_limit: The experiment demonstrates a conditional mechanism, not that fragmentation always helps or that all ancient skills have this task structure.

sources.title: The Distributional Approach: A New Way to Identify Marketplace Exchange in the Archaeological Record
sources.work_type: unavailable article; primary publisher abstract lead
sources.inspected_scope: Publisher search-rendered abstract/metadata only. Direct acquisition403 returned a challenge; no article body read.
sources.mechanism_summary: Domestic assemblage distributions are proposed as evidence of marketplace exchange.
sources.author_recommendation: No prescription beyond the abstract-level proposed method is used.
sources.interpretive_limit: Excluded from the primary selected census and from detailed trade-mechanism claims.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Bad Year Economics: Cultural Responses to Risk and Uncertainty
sources.citation: Cambridge University Press; print29 September1989; online26 October2009
sources.work_type: publisher description of edited research volume
sources.inspected_scope: Primary publisher book description and bibliographic information only; excerpt retrieval timed out twice. No chapter or whole-book reading.
sources.mechanism_summary: The description identifies mobility, economic diversification, storage and exchange as responses to spatially/temporally variable food shortage.
sources.author_recommendation: No chapter-specific prescription extracted.
sources.interpretive_limit: Contextual lead outside the 25-primary-work census; its description does not supply quantitative provisioning or trade results.

sources.title: A Model of General Economic Equilibrium
sources.inspected_scope: Printed pp1–2/PDF1–2: model setup, goods producing goods, wear stages and timing; remaining equilibrium proof not read.
sources.mechanism_summary: Circular production, joint products and stages of capital wear enter a simultaneous goods-and-process model.
sources.author_recommendation: The opening identifies interpretation questions; no practical governance prescription extracted.
sources.interpretive_limit: The model assumes constant returns and unlimited expansion of natural factors including labor, with income above necessities reinvested. It does not resolve finite archaeological work capacities.
sources.edition_note: English article footnote reports original German publication1938 and a1932 presentation; original German witness not inspected.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Production of Commodities by Means of Commodities: Prelude to a Critique of Economic Theory
sources.citation: Original work1960; inspected Indian edition1963, Vora & Co. Publishers, Bombay
sources.work_type: original economic reproduction framework; later edition witness
sources.inspected_scope: Title/copyright PDF1–2 and ChapterI printed pp3–5/PDF15–17 visually inspected; selected OCR aids inspection. Printed p6 acquired/OCR only, not used for a substantive ChapterII claim. No complete book reading.
sources.mechanism_summary: A self-replacing economy must recreate material inputs and redistribute them among mutually dependent production processes.
sources.author_recommendation: No separate future-research prescription in inspected ChapterI.
sources.interpretive_limit: The illustrated self-replacing system is an assumed case, not a claim that every city is self-sufficient or that finite labor, access and institutions are already modeled.
sources.edition_note: Image-only scan: title page identifies Vora & Co., Bombay; copyright page says Indian edition1963 and copyright1960. File stem retains first-work year.

sources.title: Note: Some Conditions of Macroeconomic Stability
sources.inspected_scope: All four pages of the note, printed pp245–248/PDF1–4, inspected through institutional scan and extracted text. No modern generalization or empirical coefficient estimate attempted.
sources.mechanism_summary: A linear production system must meet intermediate demands and final consumption together; the note provides a positivity criterion under its sign assumptions.
sources.author_recommendation: The note corrects an earlier sufficient-condition error and gives a method for checking its production equations.
sources.interpretive_limit: The interpretation assumes enough fixed factors. It does not establish workforce availability, deadlines, storage or governance for a historical city.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Resilience as pathway diversity: linking systems, individual, and temporal perspectives on resilience
sources.work_type: original conceptual model and illustrative formal examples
sources.inspected_scope: Publisher sections Resilience as Pathway Diversity, Feedbacks from Actions, agricultural planning illustration/limitations, causal entropy and poverty trap example, selected discussion and conclusion.
supporting_loci: Resilience as Pathway Diversity; Feedbacks from Actions
Agricultural Planning: guiding decision-making and limitations
sources.mechanism_summary: Choices change future access to choices; livelihood pathways have a defined horizon and are constrained by assets, relationships and feedback.
sources.author_recommendation: Refine with realistic dynamics and uncertainty, probabilistic drivers and participatory assessment, and report whose options are being counted.
sources.interpretive_limit: The agricultural example is intentionally invented; maximizing a powerful actor’s options may harm others. Pathway diversity is not a universal welfare measure.

sources.title: Operationalizing pathway diversity in a mosaic landscape
sources.inspected_scope: Publisher abstract, single-strategy results, discussion subsections on switching/abandonment/scale, reflections and conclusions. No independent model rerun or whole supplementary-data audit.
supporting_loci: Lessons from a Pathway Diversity Approach
Reflections on the Pathway Diversity Approach
sources.mechanism_summary: Accessibility matrices, collective strategies and supporting pairs can alter livelihood options, while individual gains can erode a landscape outcome.
sources.author_recommendation: Test uncertainty in matrix entries, social/environmental feedbacks, contested power contexts, co-production and trade-offs across actors and scales.
sources.interpretive_limit: One Swedish landscape and exploratory assumptions do not supply universal rankings. Short versus long horizons can reverse comparisons.

sources.title: Mesoamerican urbanism revisited: Environmental change, adaptation, resilience, persistence, and collapse
sources.citation: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 120(31):e2211558120; online24 July2023
sources.work_type: author archaeological synthesis and research agenda
sources.inspected_scope: Primary abstract and first two paragraphs each of Risk/Adaptation/Resilience, Sustainability and Adaptation, and Ongoing Research/New Research Dialogue. Full case reports and supplements not independently inspected.
supporting_loci: Ongoing Research and a New Research Dialogue, paragraphs1–2
sources.mechanism_summary: Comparative examples include dispersed reservoirs, food imports and local intensive farming, with governance and settlement layouts affecting adaptation.
sources.author_recommendation: Build cross-cultural and cross-temporal comparisons using diverse cases and material/social infrastructure, with collaboration across disciplines.
sources.interpretive_limit: These are the authors’ synthesis of other case reports. The survey does not adopt every causal attribution to autocracy or authenticate service quantities from the synthesis alone.

sources.title: Out of Order: Understanding Repair and Maintenance
sources.work_type: original urban maintenance argument and synthesis
sources.inspected_scope: Selected printed pp4–6/PDF5–7 independently read from the review agent’s retained primary-paper witness; broader urban claims on later pages depend on reviewer reading and are not included as new inspection here.
sources.mechanism_summary: Repair uses skilled apprenticeship and improvisation; maintaining service can change materials and methods and generate innovation.
sources.author_recommendation: Treat repair, maintenance and their practical knowledge as objects of social/urban inquiry.
sources.interpretive_limit: The selected qualitative argument already connects repair to innovation and practical learning. It supplies no ancient repair cadence or measured input requirement.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems
sources.citation: Nobel lecture8 December2009; Les Prix Nobel printed pp408 onward
sources.inspected_scope: Printed pp411–412/PDF4–5 and p420/PDF13 independently read from reviewer’s official lecture witness. The related2010 American Economic Review article is not an independently inspected work.
sources.mechanism_summary: Local direct providers and shared indirect services can complement one another; information, choice, aggregation and payoff rules affect action.
sources.author_recommendation: Investigate polycentric arrangements empirically and distinguish institutional rules, rather than assuming one organizing level.
sources.interpretive_limit: Modern water/police examples support alternative mechanisms; they are not evidence of ancient institutions or technical feasibility alone.
sources.edition_note: The official lecture heading uses Complex Economic Systems; citation to the later AER version sometimes uses a different title. This record is the2009 lecture witness.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: The Cost of Restoration as a Way of Defining Resilience: a Viability Approach Applied to a Model of Lake Eutrophication
sources.work_type: original viability model and operational resilience definition
sources.inspected_scope: Primary abstract, Methods opening through objectives/time horizon, cost-function subsection and selected discussion; reused coordinator HTML. Numerical lake experiment and proof appendices not independently reproduced.
supporting_loci: Methods > Mathematical Formulation > dynamics and controls
Methods > cost function, disturbance and resilience
sources.mechanism_summary: The viable subset contains states admitting at least one control trajectory that meets the chosen property through the horizon; restoration costs depend on the property and disturbance.
sources.author_recommendation: Specify property, controls, disturbance, horizon and cost when making resilience operational.
sources.interpretive_limit: The selected law assumes the controlling institution can bear control changes and treats those provider costs as external to its chosen resilience cost. A broader boundary requires additional resource accounting.

sources.title: Thinking Through Change: Combining the Adaptive Cycle and Assemblage Theory to Assess Urban Change in Later Medieval Northern England
sources.citation: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory; DOI10.1007/s10816-026-09803-2
sources.inspected_scope: Primary publisher web-rendered selected lines146–191,296–310,368–376 and397–404 independently read through coordinator captures. Direct HTML was a challenge; no full PDF or complete article read.
sources.mechanism_summary: Yards and boundaries persist through repeated maintenance, changing relations and materials; archaeological phases can conceal overlapping temporal processes.
sources.author_recommendation: Compare material relations and consider integration with empirical network analysis, including Priß et al.2026.
sources.interpretive_limit: Invisible maintenance and temporal/boundary complexity are explicit prior arguments. Interpretation of a persistent yard does not itself measure total work, service output or the unique mechanism.

sources.title: Integrating Restoration and Scheduling Decisions for Disrupted Interdependent Infrastructure Systems
sources.citation: Annals of Operations Research 203:279–294; author page reports online-first5 September2011
sources.work_type: original mathematical optimization model and computational application
sources.inspected_scope: Author manuscript selected abstract and pp3–4,7 independently read from reviewer witness. Publication chronology is from retained author-page capture; no whole model/computational results rerun.
sources.mechanism_summary: Restoration task selection, work-group assignment, scheduling and infrastructure dependencies are solved together with service performance over time.
sources.author_recommendation: Integrate planning and scheduling rather than sequentially optimizing installation cost and task completion; offer usable heuristic methods.
sources.interpretive_limit: This is a direct predecessor for shared repair resources and joint plans. Modern task durations and management assumptions do not identify ancient ones.
sources.recommendation_status: methodological framing or stated objective, not a separate future-research prescription

sources.title: Urban resilience in Ancient Mesopotamia: insights into the socioeconomic system of the Bronze and Iron Age Khabur Valley
sources.inspected_scope: Publisher PDF title/abstract/intro p340, route reconstruction p342 and metric assumptions p345/PDF1,3,6. References on p352 viewed but not used as inspected evidence. No complete article/code or result reanalysis.
sources.mechanism_summary: Reconstructed settlement/route graphs provide period-specific connectivity and potential proxies for adaptive-cycle comparisons.
sources.author_recommendation: Operationalize the cycle with testable network expectations; include settlement diversity/specialization when data permit.
sources.interpretive_limit: Hollow ways are hard to date; missing sites/routes are reconstructed and size can be held constant. The selected metrics are proxies, not measured imports, repair capacity or a unique causal history.
